I did a lot of research into solar PV systems before signing up with e-Solar in December 2018, and read a lot of reviews online. I came to realise that, apart from buying a good quality inverter and decent solar panels, the after-sales service and support of the company from which one buys the system is of paramount importance. E-Solar and its owner, Silvio, got excellent reviews, and all my communications with Silvio make me feel confident that I had found someone who cares about his customers and who would be on the doorstep if any problems arose after installation. Silvio was incredibly patient in answering all my questions in the 5-week period between signing up and the date set for installation in January, and I always received prompt email answers to my questions. So I felt confident in signing off on a 5.3kW system with 16 Trina Tallmax panels with e-Solar.On installation day, however, everything went pear-shaped. The subcontracted installer took one look at my complicated double-storey townhouse roof with wavy Tuscan-style roof tiles, announced that he could only fit 8 panels on it instead of the 16 specified, and left. Once Iâ€™d recovered from the shock, I began to realise that placing little rectangles representing panels on the NearMap aerial image is only an estimation of how many panels will fit on a roof, not a substitute for a site inspection and measure up. Communication between Silvio and the installer as to the nature of the job also appeared to have been lacking. The installer didnâ€™t know what to expect or what equipment to bring with him because no-one had looked at the job beforehand and he hadnâ€™t been properly briefed. Apart from 16 panels not fitting, he didnâ€™t have long enough roof brackets for the wavy roof tiles and also was extremely reluctant to work on the precipitous NE facing roof (which was one of two optimal positions for the panels and my preferred option).As the planned 5.3kW system was out of the question, Silvio went into damage control mode and offered a 3.15kW system with 10 physically smaller Risen panels. This probably would have done an adequate job in covering self-consumption, but by that stage Iâ€™d lost confidence in both Silvio for not scoping the job accurately as well as the installer who was dragging his heels. I really didnâ€™t want him to come back, even though Silvio said heâ€™d persuaded him to do the job of installing a smaller system. Also, the original design of all panels facing NW with some on a lower garage roof I had felt all along was not ideal. Without a site visit, it is difficult to see that this lower roof is shaded by trees starting at 4.15pm (summer) and only gets full sun around midday as there is a double-storey wall partially blocking the sun. So the efficiency of the lower panel array would be compromised, and the second array on the house roof was never going to generate even 3kW on its own. Silvio was adamant that utilising the high NE-facing roof for a second array was not a good idea as it could only accommodate 5 panels which he told me would not start the inverter (and the installer was refusing to work on the steep NE roof anyway).At that point, I decided to take some time out to rethink the feasibility of getting solar as there seemed to be so many problems. Silvio was very apologetic and was quick to refund my deposit. In a last ditch attempt to salvage something but feeling less than optimistic after my experience with e-Solar, I called another small company who, to my surprise, actually insisted on sending someone to get up on the roof before they would even quote. Two weeks later they installed a 3.78kW system of 12 panels without any problems utilising both the NW and NE roofs, the optimal orientation for the panels which I had been told by Silvio would not work. The Goodwe inverter starts at sunrise and runs until sunset and the app shows that it produces on average 22kWh per day on sunny days, a great result.I felt very let down by e-Solar but, to be fair, it was a less-than-straightforward install. This would have been apparent if a site inspection had been done, and therein lies the problem. If you have a simple Colorbond roof with room for a couple of long straight lines of panel arrays, youâ€™ll be fine. Anything more complex, make sure you have a site visit to have your roof measured up and the tiles checked out so that you know what can or canâ€™t be done before the installer turns up. The issue about the inverter not starting with only 5 panels on a string was clearly not correct too as itâ€™s working perfectly and I suspect was a way of justifying not working on a steep, tight roof area.
